overview: This file documents Japan’s evolving system of immigration control, alien registration, labor restriction, and overseas migration between 1931 and 1939, while incorporating translations of regulations dating back to 1899. It covers metropolitan Japan, colonial Taiwan, and the South Seas Mandate; examines Chinese labor migration, foreign performers and temporary workers, alien landownership, Japanese settlement in Brazil and Manchuria, and international restrictions on Japanese migrants; and records American consular efforts to interpret and respond to Japanese policy. The collection culminates in Japan’s comprehensive 1939 ordinance governing foreigners’ entry, residence, travel, policing, and deportation.
interest: The file is especially useful for showing that immigration control rested not only on published law but also on police discretion and administrative practice, particularly in the exclusion of alien laborers and restriction of Chinese landholding. Its combination of translated laws, blank administrative forms, statistical appendices, internal memoranda, and diplomatic correspondence lets historians compare formal rules with their everyday implementation across Japan’s imperial territories. The President Jefferson dispute offers an unusually detailed case study of how a minor boarding misunderstanding became a diplomatic incident, while the discussion rejecting American “retaliation in kind” reveals how officials evaluated reciprocity and discrimination on the eve of the Pacific War.
